recent_posts.title: Control the Speed of Infinite Animations
recent_posts.summary: A technique for controlling the speed of infinite CSS animations using `animation-composition: add`. By running the same animation twice with an additive effect and pausing/resuming the second instance via a CSS variable, you can make animations faster, slower, or reverse direction on hover or other interactions. Examples include infinite rotation, a marquee using `offset-distance`, and a glowing border effect animating a CSS variable. A fallback without `if()` is also provided for broader browser support.

recent_posts.title: The Lazy Tooltip Follower
recent_posts.summary: A CSS demo showing how to create a 'lazy' tooltip that follows its anchor element with a delay, using CSS Anchor Positioning and transitions on inset properties. A second variation uses the linear() easing function to achieve a bouncy effect.

recent_posts.title: Hand-Drawn Underline using border-shape
recent_posts.summary: A tutorial on creating hand-drawn style underlines for menu items using the modern CSS border-shape property, offering a decorative UI technique with minimal markup.

recent_posts.title: Convert Complex SVG Shapes into CSS
recent_posts.summary: An SVG-to-CSS converter tool has been updated to support multiple SVG path elements, not just a single path. It merges multiple path elements by concatenating their 'd' attribute values and converts them into a single CSS shape() function, producing responsive single-element code. A border-only version using border-shape is also available (Chrome-only). The technique works when paths form separate portions of the same shape, share the same color, and have no transforms applied. The author emphasizes that shape() is not a replacement for SVG but a proof-of-concept tool.

recent_posts.title: How to use border-shape to create CSS shapes with borders and shadows
recent_posts.summary: The new CSS `border-shape` property offers a powerful way to create shapes while preserving decorations like borders, shadows, and outlines — something `clip-path` and `mask` cannot do. It accepts the same value syntax as `clip-path` (polygon(), shape(), inset(), circle(), etc.), making it easy to adopt. Currently available in Chrome 147+, it complements rather than replaces existing methods: `mask` remains useful for repeating patterns and `clip-path` for clipping/reveal effects. Several CSS shape generators have been updated to provide border-shape versions.

recent_posts.title: Sliding "Liquid Oozing" Reveal Effect
recent_posts.summary: A tutorial on creating a liquid oozing reveal animation using CSS clip-path with the shape() function. The technique involves using a wavy divider generator to produce two shapes with matching granularity and shape IDs, enabling the browser to smoothly transition between them for a fluid visual effect.

recent_posts.title: CSS-only Chrome Dino Game
recent_posts.summary: A CSS-only recreation of the Chrome Dino game, fully playable with keyboard arrow keys for jumping and crouching. Built using modern CSS features including Scroll-Driven Animations, @property, and container queries. Currently works only in Chrome.

recent_posts.title: The Gotcha of using counter() with container
recent_posts.summary: When you add `container-type` to an element in CSS, it implicitly applies style containment, which scopes CSS counters. This means descendants can no longer access `counter-reset` defined on the container or outside it. The result is that `counter-increment` inside the container creates a new isolated counter per element instead of sharing one, causing unexpected behavior. The fix is either to move `counter-reset` onto the container element itself or to move `counter-increment` to the actual elements rather than pseudo-elements. The same issue applies when using `contain: style`, `strict`, or `content`.

recent_posts.title: Add a Wobbling Animation to your Images
recent_posts.summary: A short CSS tip showing how to create an infinite wobbling animation for images using the CSS `shape()` function and `clip-path`. The technique uses a single element with simple code, requiring three shapes generated at the same granularity to ensure smooth transitions between them. A fancy frames generator tool is referenced to simplify shape creation.

recent_posts.title: A Squishy Button with a Hover/Click Effect
recent_posts.summary: A tutorial on creating a squishy button with hover and click animations using the CSS `shape()` function. The technique involves generating multiple shape states with a specific relationship between size and radius values (their sum must remain constant), using an online generator at css-generators.com/fancy-frame to produce the required CSS code. Three shape states are defined to create the squish animation effect.
